INSM: Sells Arikayce, an inhaled antibiotic for a rare chronic lung infection, and Brinsupri, approved in 2025 as the first drug for bronchiectasis — a disease with no prior treatment and a large diagnosed population.
YPF: Argentina's oil company, majority controlled by the state since 2012. The growth is Vaca Muerta shale; the risk is that the same state also sets domestic fuel prices.
EWZ: Index fund holding the largest Brazilian listings — Petrobras, Vale, the banks — so it trades as a position on commodity prices and Brazilian rates rather than on any one company.
TBBB: Runs Tiendas 3B, a hard-discount grocery chain in Mexico stocking a few hundred mostly private-label items per store. The model is low prices on a narrow assortment, one small store at a time.
AA: Mines bauxite, refines it into alumina and smelts primary aluminium, so earnings swing with the metal price and with the cost of the electricity smelting consumes.
NAMS: Developing obicetrapib, an oral CETP inhibitor that lowers LDL cholesterol on top of a statin; partnered with Menarini in Europe and dependent on cardiovascular outcomes, not on the lipid numbers alone.
STM: Makes microcontrollers, analog and power chips — silicon carbide included — for cars and factories, where a design win lasts a model cycle and the cycle is currently the problem.
WWD: Makes fuel systems, actuation and control hardware for aircraft engines and industrial turbines. The aftermarket on engines already flying is worth more than the original equipment.
TEVA: The largest generic drug manufacturer in the world, now leaning on branded products — Austedo, Ajovy, Uzedy — to carry margins while it works down the debt left by the Allergan generics acquisition.
CPNG: Korea's dominant online retailer, which owns its warehouses and delivery fleet rather than renting them, and sells a membership that makes next-morning delivery the default.
OPCH: Delivers infusion therapy at home or in its own clinics instead of a hospital, billing insurers for the drug and the nursing; the growth comes from payers preferring the cheaper site of care.
FIGR: Originates home equity lines of credit and records them on its own Provenance blockchain, which lets the loans be funded and sold in days rather than weeks. Most revenue comes from originating and selling loans, not from holding them.
ARGT: Index fund holding the Argentine listings — the banks, the energy names, YPF — and therefore a position on Argentine policy more than on any company in it.
CAI: Sequences tumours for oncologists to guide treatment choice, and licenses the resulting clinical-genomic database to drug developers. The testing is the revenue; the accumulated data is the asset.
QSR: Franchises Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs, collecting a royalty on system-wide sales rather than operating most of the restaurants itself.
RVMD: Developing RAS(ON) inhibitors — daraxonrasib first, in pancreatic and lung cancer — against the mutation that has resisted drugging for forty years. Nothing approved yet.
LSCC: Sells small low-power FPGAs, the programmable chips that sit beside a main processor handling glue logic, control and security in servers, industrial gear and communications equipment.
UAL: One of the three US network carriers, where the profit now comes from premium cabins, the transatlantic network and the co-branded credit card rather than from coach fares.
HUM: Sells Medicare Advantage plans and increasingly owns the clinics treating the members. Profit is the spread between the government's fixed per-member payment and what that member's care actually costs.
WAB: Builds and services freight locomotives and the braking systems on rail and transit equipment; the size of the installed base makes the aftermarket the steadier half.
TWLO: Sells APIs that let software send text messages, place calls and verify logins, billed per message — so revenue tracks how much its customers' own users do, not how many seats they buy.
GSG: A trust holding futures on the S&P GSCI commodity index, which is energy-heavy by construction, so it moves with crude oil far more than with commodities as a group.
CLF: Mines iron ore and rolls flat steel for carmakers, which levers it twice to one cycle: the price of steel and the volume Detroit orders.
NUVB: Sells Ibtrozi, approved in 2025 for ROS1-positive lung cancer — a mutation-defined population small enough that one approval can carry a company.
BLTE: Developing tinlarebant, an oral drug meant to slow retinal damage in Stargardt disease and geographic atrophy by limiting the vitamin A byproducts that accumulate in the eye.
PTGX: Designs peptide drugs and partners them out rather than selling them itself: rusfertide for polycythemia vera with Takeda, an oral IL-23 blocker with Johnson & Johnson.
U: Sells the game engine most mobile studios build on, plus the ad network that monetises the games built with it. The engine is the position; the advertising is the revenue.
OLMA: Developing palazestrant, an oral drug that degrades the oestrogen receptor in ER-positive breast cancer, for patients whose tumours have stopped responding to existing hormonal therapy.
Q: The electronics business DuPont spun off in November 2025: the materials chipmakers consume in the fab — polishing slurries, photoresists — plus the interconnect materials carrying signals inside a package.
ADMA: Makes immunoglobulin therapies from human plasma collected at its own donation centres, which is unusual — most of the industry buys the plasma it fractionates.
XENE: Developing azetukalner, a potassium channel opener for epilepsy and depression. It is the most advanced drug of its mechanism, which is both the opportunity and the risk.
JBS: The largest meat company in the world — beef, poultry and pork across Brazil, the US and Australia — which moved its primary listing to New York in 2025.
DAKT: Builds the LED scoreboards and video displays in stadiums, arenas and along highways, sold as projects rather than as product, so the backlog says more than the quarter does.
LYB: Makes polyethylene and polypropylene — the plastics in packaging and pipe — and licenses the processes for making them. Margin is the spread between resin prices and feedstock gas.
VIST: Pumps shale oil from Vaca Muerta in Argentina, the one basin where output is still growing quickly, and exports most of what it produces.
COHR: Makes the optical transceivers and lasers that carry traffic between switches inside a data centre, which is where the AI build-out shows up as unit volume.
CLS: Assembles hardware for other companies, increasingly the networking switches and racks hyperscalers design themselves — a contract manufacturer whose revenue is its customers' capital spending.
STUB: Runs the resale marketplace for event tickets, taking a fee from both buyer and seller on each transaction. It holds no inventory and lists whatever fans and brokers put on it.
DBVT: Developing Viaskin Peanut, a skin patch meant to desensitise peanut-allergic children through the skin rather than by having them swallow the allergen.
ECHO: What is left of Dish: Boost Mobile as a wireless brand riding AT&T's towers and Starlink's satellites, plus satellite TV, Sling and Hughes broadband — the spectrum that was the real asset having been sold to AT&T and SpaceX.
ALM: Mines tungsten, most of it from the Sangdong deposit in South Korea that began commercial production in 2025. The appeal is that nearly all existing tungsten supply comes from China.
PCT: Purifies waste polypropylene back into a resin usable like virgin plastic. One plant in Ohio, and the question has always been whether it runs at rate.
SOLS: The materials business Honeywell spun off in 2025: low global-warming refrigerants, which are most of the revenue, plus semiconductor materials, protective fibres and healthcare packaging.
WLK: Makes PVC and chlor-alkali chemicals and the pipe, siding and windows built from them, so both halves of the company answer to US housing.
WVE: Designs oligonucleotides that edit or silence RNA, with programmes in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and obesity. All still clinical.
